newsitem.title: UK: Analysts see positive outlook for Provident.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see positive outlook for Provident.

text.p: British credit and insurance group Provident Financial Plc has a bright outlook as long as it does not rely on organic growth of its core lending business, analysts said on Tuesday.
The company, which holds its annual general meeting on Thursday, lends money to those deemed uncreditworthy by high street banks.

"I honestly do not believe there is any significant medium-term organic growth left in home-collected credit," said John Marr, financial companies analyst at Charterhouse Tilney. "They desperately need to make an acquisition."

Provident said in February it was considering growth by acquisition and a possible share buyback as ways of improving shareholder value. The company is also a big player in the motor insurance market, a possible area for expansion.
Marr, however, did not think Provident had yet found a suitor of high enough calibre to make a match. Neither did he or other analysts think a share buyback was likely.
"I think that's very unlikely, they've reduced their dividend cover," said Robert Mumby at BZW.
Provident has been something of a success story on the London Stock Exchange in recent years and is currently around the low 120s in the list of the largest UK-listed companies.
It posted a 17 percent rise in its 1996 pre-tax profits to 118.5 million stg and has enjoyed remarkable growth of an average 26 percent over the last five years.
Marr said Provident had seen its profitability boosted by a cost-cutting exercise which had seen around 300 branches closed, though he said these were largely one-off measures.
"Most of the increase in profitability in the last five years has really been down to the cost-cutting exercise."
Provident has also come under increased competition from rival moneylender Cattles Plc whose Shopacheck weekly home-collected credit business increased its customer base by 16,000 in 1996.

But Provident would likely continue to generate healthy profits given its prime position in the mass money lending market, while a large cash pile and city confidence in the management team would support investor confidence.

The company would suffer from any hint of a clampdown on their high interest rate lending by a possible incoming Labour government in Britain, Marr said. But, he added, the company's executive chairman John van Kuffeler had handled this situation well.

"The sector, and in particular, Provident is very aware of this and handles the political lobbying expertly," he said of a possible future clamp down on their lending, adding: "They do not see it remotely as a threat."
